inside_front_cover.heading: A NOTE FROM MANAGEMENT
memo: Thank you for choosing Drain Damage. Your service call is important to us, particularly if it can be billed at the emergency rate.

Our technicians will make every reasonable effort to restore your plumbing and locate any guests displaced by it. Please keep the service entrance clear. If the service entrance has become a drain, please indicate this on the form.
Wedding cakes are not load-bearing. We mention this because it has come up before.

story_pages.layout: Right-hand page. Upper-half establishing image, three smaller panels below.
panels: Luxury hotel entrance decorated for wedding; Tony and Sean approach. Tony wears the backpack jetter with nozzle secured, switched off; Sean carries the long-handled plunger shown on the cover and a service kit. Title: SOMETHING BORROWED, SOMETHING SPEWED. BJ radio: The hotel has lost water pressure. They need it restored before the ceremony.

At the entrance mat, equipment set safely beside them, both put disposable white boot covers over their boots before entering. Sean looks toward staff setting up the ceremony. Sean: They’re already seating people. Tony: Let’s find the manager.

Both now wear white boot covers. Tony checks job details on his phone; Sean has picked up his plunger and service kit. Tony: Any maintenance notes, BJ? BJ radio: Nothing on file. The manager says the plumbing’s immaculate.
Their white-covered boots meet the manager’s polished shoes at the pristine cream carpet. BJ radio: They’ve approved the emergency rate. Take your time.

story_pages.layout: Left of spread. Wide top panel, two medium panels, two smaller panels.
panels: Manager leads heroes beside ballroom; beverage tap dribbles behind them. Manager: We’ve just completed a substantial refurbishment. Tony: Did that include the plumbing? Manager: It included everything the guests can see.

Water creeps beneath the service door toward a power strip and tangled cables on the floor. Its lead runs to a wall socket; a small indicator light is on. Sean stops short and looks toward Tony with worried disbelief. His mouth opens, but words fail him.

Sean stays clear of the approaching water and points at the power strip, looking to Tony for confirmation that this place is as bad as it looks. Sean, small hesitant balloon: Uh… Tony: Good catch. Tony’s distracted scan stops at the strip. He turns to the manager. Tony: We need the power off here. Who has access to the breaker panel? His expression reflects decades of experience recognizing a wider maintenance problem.

The manager takes out his phone. Tony shines his light through the cupboard opening from the dry side of the doorway: old pipes and decorating supplies hastily shoved out of sight. Manager: I’ll get maintenance. We were assured the repair would last through the reception.
Tony looks down with professional disbelief, no smirk. Tony: Who assured you?

story_pages.layout: Right of spread. Five panels; large pipe reveal, quiet final strip. Monster hidden until page turn.
panels: A split pipe is buried beneath overlapping gray duct tape. Wet edges peel away; a thin stream escapes between layers into a puddle. Beside it, the manager sweats and gives a guilty, strained grin as he tries to tuck a matching roll of duct tape into his jacket pocket. The roll remains plainly visible to the reader. This silently answers Tony’s page-2 question, Who assured you? No dialogue.

Sean’s eyes move from the leaking repair to the roll disappearing into the manager’s pocket. He looks at Tony in disbelieving recognition. Tony follows his glance and holds a weary look on the manager. No dialogue; let their expressions land the discovery.

Tony follows the pipe with his light from the dry side of the doorway, then addresses the manager. The guilty grin fades. Tony: Where’s the main water shutoff? Manager: Downstairs, in the basement mechanical room. I—

Every toilet in the nearby bathroom flushes at once, cutting the manager off mid-sentence. Large SFX: FWHOOOOSH. All three turn. Sean: Was somebody in there? Manager: It’s been closed since breakfast.
Bathroom doorway with heroes looking toward empty row of stalls. One stall emits small SFX: …glug. No dialogue.

story_pages.layout: After page turn. Reveal occupies upper two-thirds; three small action panels below.
panels: Flushfiend breaks out of stall, pipe legs against tile, ceramic teeth visible. Tony and scared Sean establish scale in foreground. SFX: KRRRAK. Sean: Tony. The toilet has teeth. Tony: I see them.

Tony plants himself between the Flushfiend and the corridor, thrusting an arm toward the ballroom to direct the manager away. He SHOUTS with urgent, unmistakable authority, eyes fixed on the threat. Tony, strong emphatic lettering: GET EVERYONE OUT OF THIS CORRIDOR! The manager recoils, wide-eyed and pale, his hands flying up. He looks toward the approaching wedding party in panic. Manager, shaky shout balloon: Oh God—the wedding! They’re right outside!
Sean closes bathroom entrance and braces door with plunger handle as creature lunges. Sean: Tony, a little help!
Tony joins Sean holding door; ceramic tooth punches through between them. BJ radio: Have you located the blockage? Tony: It’s trying to leave.

Page 3 silently implicates the sweating, guiltily grinning manager via the duct-tape roll he conceals. This replaces the maintenance-supervisor assurance. No dialogue names someone else as the repairer. Tony asks for the main water shutoff; manager identifies basement mechanical room and is interrupted by simultaneous flushing. Keep both heroes clear of the wet electrical hazard.

Hotel main domestic-water shutoff is in the basement mechanical room at the service entry/meter assembly. Plausible fictional layout, not a universal hotel rule; local branch isolation valves may also exist. Do not confuse domestic water with fire-suppression controls.
Page 4 panel 2: Tony takes command with a shouted evacuation order; the manager reacts in visible panic with a shaky exclamation, not a calm conversational reply. Use lettering and acting together.

dialogue_direction: Develop sustained conversations, character-specific voice, meaningful exposition and variable speech length. Avoid every panel ending in a short quip. Rising Stars is a reference for substantial dialogue, not a request to imitate wording. Emphasis and exclamation cannot substitute for believable panic.
